::: {.objectives}
**Goals.** Read real elevation and land-cover rasters; derive terrain
covariates; annotate the buffalo track; compare used with available; see how
the answer changes with buffer radius; and build a **time-matched**
annotation.

**Time:** ~55 minutes. **Packages:** `terra`, `sf`, `amt`, `dplyr`.
:::


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
library(terra)
library(sf)
library(amt)
library(dplyr)
library(tidyr)
library(lubridate)
```
:::


## Task 1 — The rasters


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
elev <- rast("data/kruger_elevation.tif")
lc   <- rast("data/kruger_landcover.tif")

elev
#> class       : SpatRaster
#> size        : 168, 132, 1  (nrow, ncol, nlyr)
#> resolution  : 0.008333333, 0.008333333  (x, y)
#> extent      : 31.4, 32.5, -25.3, -23.9  (xmin, xmax, ymin, ymax)
#> coord. ref. : lon/lat WGS 84 (EPSG:4326)
#> source      : kruger_elevation.tif
#> name        : elevation
#> min value   :       117
#> max value   :       572
names(lc)
#> [1] "trees"     "grassland" "shrubs"    "cropland"
```
:::


`lc` holds ESA WorldCover **fractional cover** per 30 arc-second cell: the
proportion of each cell that is trees, grassland, shrubs or cropland.


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
plot(c(elev, lc[["trees"]], lc[["grassland"]], lc[["shrubs"]]),
     col = hcl.colors(50, "Viridis"), nc = 2)
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![](exercise_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-4-1.png){fig-align='center' width=864}
:::
:::


### Your turn

**1a.** Do the two rasters share a CRS, extent and resolution?
**1b.** What fraction of the area is dominated by grassland (> 0.5)?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Solution


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
c(elev = crs(elev, describe = TRUE)$code, lc = crs(lc, describe = TRUE)$code)
#>   elev     lc 
#> "4326" "4326"
ext(elev); ext(lc)
#> SpatExtent : 31.4, 32.5, -25.3, -23.9 (xmin, xmax, ymin, ymax)
#> SpatExtent : 31.3999999999942, 32.4999999999941, -25.299999999997, -23.899999999997 (xmin, xmax, ymin, ymax)
res(elev); res(lc)
#> [1] 0.008333333 0.008333333
#> [1] 0.008333333 0.008333333

global(lc[["grassland"]] > 0.5, "mean", na.rm = TRUE)
#>                mean
#> grassland 0.4007486
```
:::


Same CRS, same resolution — and extents that agree **to within floating-point
noise**: `lc` reports `31.3999999999942` where `elev` reports `31.4`. `terra`
tolerates a discrepancy that small and stacks them happily, which is why
`c(elev, lc)` works in Task 2.

Do not rely on that. In real work rasters come from different providers on
genuinely different grids, and you must align them explicitly — `project()` to
a common CRS, then `resample()` one onto the other's grid. Always align
*before* stacking, never after.
:::

## Task 2 — Derived terrain covariates

Raw elevation is rarely the thing an animal responds to. Slope and ruggedness
usually are.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
terr <- terrain(elev, v = c("slope", "TRI"), unit = "degrees")
names(terr) <- c("slope", "tri")

covs <- c(elev, terr, lc)
names(covs)
#> [1] "elevation" "slope"     "tri"       "trees"     "grassland" "shrubs"   
#> [7] "cropland"
```
:::



::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
plot(terr, col = hcl.colors(50, "Inferno"), nc = 2)
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![](exercise_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-7-1.png){fig-align='center' width=768}
:::
:::


::: {.callout-tip}
**TRI** (terrain ruggedness index) is the mean absolute difference between a
cell and its neighbours. For animals it often matters more than slope: a
uniformly steep hillside is easy to traverse, a broken one is not.
:::

## Task 3 — Annotate the track


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
clean <- read.csv("data/buffalo_kruger.csv.gz") |>
  transmute(id = individual.local.identifier,
            t  = as.POSIXct(timestamp, tz = "UTC"),
            x  = location.long, y = location.lat) |>
  filter(!is.na(x), !is.na(y)) |>
  distinct(id, t, .keep_all = TRUE)

trk <- make_track(clean, x, y, t, id = id, crs = 4326)

used <- trk |>
  st_as_sf(coords = c("x_", "y_"), crs = 4326) |>
  bind_cols(terra::extract(covs, vect(
    st_as_sf(trk, coords = c("x_", "y_"), crs = 4326)
  ))[, -1])

summary(used[, c("elevation", "slope", "trees", "grassland")] |> st_drop_geometry())
#>    elevation         slope             trees           grassland     
#>  Min.   :148.0   Min.   :0.03109   Min.   :0.00000   Min.   :0.0000  
#>  1st Qu.:239.0   1st Qu.:0.35321   1st Qu.:0.00000   1st Qu.:0.8622  
#>  Median :265.0   Median :0.47231   Median :0.00040   Median :0.9624  
#>  Mean   :260.5   Mean   :0.60465   Mean   :0.02831   Mean   :0.9000  
#>  3rd Qu.:287.0   3rd Qu.:0.62735   3rd Qu.:0.03440   3rd Qu.:0.9956  
#>  Max.   :422.0   Max.   :5.41180   Max.   :0.86910   Max.   :1.0000  
#>  NAs    :1       NAs    :1
```
:::


### Your turn

**3a.** Now generate *available* points across the study area and annotate them too.
**3b.** Compare used vs available for each covariate. What stands out?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Solution


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
set.seed(1)

# Available = random points within the buffalo's collective range
hull <- st_convex_hull(st_union(used))
avail_pts <- st_sample(hull, size = nrow(used), type = "random")

avail <- st_sf(geometry = avail_pts) |>
  bind_cols(terra::extract(covs, vect(st_sf(geometry = avail_pts)))[, -1])

comp <- bind_rows(
  used  |> st_drop_geometry() |> select(elevation, slope, tri, trees, grassland, shrubs) |> mutate(what = "used"),
  avail |> st_drop_geometry() |> select(elevation, slope, tri, trees, grassland, shrubs) |> mutate(what = "available")
)

comp |>
  pivot_longer(-what) |>
  group_by(name, what) |>
  summarise(mean = round(mean(value, na.rm = TRUE), 3), .groups = "drop") |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = what, values_from = mean) |>
  mutate(ratio = round(used / available, 2))
#> # A tibble: 6 × 4
#>   name      available    used ratio
#>   <chr>         <dbl>   <dbl> <dbl>
#> 1 elevation   280.    260.     0.93
#> 2 grassland     0.561   0.9    1.6 
#> 3 shrubs        0.316   0.05   0.16
#> 4 slope         0.662   0.605  0.91
#> 5 trees         0.114   0.028  0.25
#> 6 tri          10.4     9.33   0.9
```
:::



::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
par(mfrow = c(2, 3))
for (v in c("elevation", "slope", "tri", "trees", "grassland", "shrubs")) {
  d_u <- density(comp[[v]][comp$what == "used"], na.rm = TRUE)
  d_a <- density(comp[[v]][comp$what == "available"], na.rm = TRUE)
  plot(d_a, col = "grey50", lwd = 2, main = v, xlab = "",
       ylim = c(0, max(d_u$y, d_a$y)))
  lines(d_u, col = "#1f6f78", lwd = 2)
  if (v == "elevation") {
    legend("topright", c("available", "used"), col = c("grey50", "#1f6f78"),
           lwd = 2, bty = "n", cex = 0.9)
  }
}
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![](exercise_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-10-1.png){fig-align='center' width=864}
:::

```{.r .cell-code}
par(mfrow = c(1, 1))
```
:::


Where the teal (used) curve sits to the right of the grey (available) curve,
the animals are using more of that covariate than the landscape offers —
**selection**. To the left is **avoidance**.

This side-by-side comparison of used and available distributions *is* the idea
behind a resource selection function. Class 7 turns it into a model that
handles several covariates at once and gives you uncertainty.
:::

## Task 4 — Point or buffer?

The scale at which you measure the environment is a hypothesis about how far
the animal can perceive. Let us ask for tree cover averaged over a
neighbourhood.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
pts <- st_as_sf(trk, coords = c("x_", "y_"), crs = 4326) |> vect()

at_point <- terra::extract(covs[["trees"]], pts)[, 2]
buf_500  <- terra::extract(covs[["trees"]], pts, buffer = 500,  fun = mean, na.rm = TRUE)[, 2]
buf_2000 <- terra::extract(covs[["trees"]], pts, buffer = 2000, fun = mean, na.rm = TRUE)[, 2]

data.frame(
  scale = c("at fix", "buffer = 500", "buffer = 2000"),
  mean  = round(c(mean(at_point,  na.rm = TRUE),
                  mean(buf_500,   na.rm = TRUE),
                  mean(buf_2000,  na.rm = TRUE)), 4),
  sd    = round(c(sd(at_point, na.rm = TRUE),
                  sd(buf_500,  na.rm = TRUE),
                  sd(buf_2000, na.rm = TRUE)), 4)
)
#>           scale   mean     sd
#> 1        at fix 0.0283 0.0553
#> 2  buffer = 500 0.0283 0.0553
#> 3 buffer = 2000 0.0283 0.0553

identical(at_point, buf_500)
#> [1] TRUE
identical(at_point, buf_2000)
#> [1] TRUE
```
:::


::: {.callout-important}
## The `buffer=` argument was silently ignored

All three columns are **identical**. In this version of `terra`
(1.9.27), passing `buffer=` to
`extract()` with point geometries does nothing at all — no error, no warning,
just the at-point values three times over.

Had you not checked, you would have reported a "multi-scale analysis" in which
every scale was the same scale.

**The habit:** when an argument is supposed to change the answer, *verify that
it did*. `identical()` costs one line.
:::

The reliable way is to build the buffer polygons yourself. Work in a projected
CRS so the radius is honestly in metres.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
covs_utm <- project(covs, "EPSG:32736")
pts_utm  <- project(pts, "EPSG:32736")

buffer_mean <- function(r, p, width) {
  terra::extract(r, buffer(p, width = width), fun = mean, na.rm = TRUE)[, 2]
}

scales <- c(500, 2000, 5000)
tab <- lapply(scales, function(w) {
  v <- buffer_mean(covs_utm[["trees"]], pts_utm, w)
  data.frame(radius_m = w, mean = mean(v, na.rm = TRUE), sd = sd(v, na.rm = TRUE))
}) |> bind_rows()

at_pt <- terra::extract(covs_utm[["trees"]], pts_utm)[, 2]

bind_rows(
  data.frame(radius_m = 0, mean = mean(at_pt, na.rm = TRUE), sd = sd(at_pt, na.rm = TRUE)),
  tab
) |> mutate(across(c(mean, sd), \(z) round(z, 4)))
#>   radius_m   mean     sd
#> 1        0 0.0280 0.0468
#> 2      500 0.0279 0.0455
#> 3     2000 0.0276 0.0342
#> 4     5000 0.0274 0.0313
```
:::


### Your turn

**4a.** What happens to the variance as the radius grows?
**4b.** Why does a 500 m radius barely differ from the point value?
**4c.** Which scale would you choose, and on what grounds?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Solution


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
b2000 <- buffer_mean(covs_utm[["trees"]], pts_utm, 2000)

par(mfrow = c(1, 2))
plot(at_pt, b2000, pch = 16, cex = 0.2, col = adjustcolor("#1f6f78", 0.2),
     xlab = "Tree cover at the fix", ylab = "Mean within 2 km",
     main = "The same covariate at two scales")
abline(0, 1, col = "firebrick", lty = 2)

plot(c(0, scales), c(sd(at_pt, na.rm = TRUE), tab$sd), type = "b", pch = 16,
     col = "#1f6f78", lwd = 2, xlab = "Buffer radius (m)",
     ylab = "SD of the covariate", main = "Smoothing destroys contrast")
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![](exercise_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-13-1.png){fig-align='center' width=816}
:::

```{.r .cell-code}
par(mfrow = c(1, 1))
```
:::


**Variance falls** as the radius grows: you are averaging over more cells, so
extremes cancel. The mean barely moves; the spread collapses.

That has a direct statistical consequence. A smoothed covariate has less
contrast between used and available points, so the **effect size you can
detect shrinks**, and a real preference can be smoothed into
non-significance.

**Why 500 m does almost nothing.** The raster cells are 30 arc-seconds —
about 900 m on the ground here:


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
round(res(covs_utm))
#> [1] 893 893
```
:::


A 500 m radius fits inside a single cell, so the "neighbourhood mean" is
mostly that one cell's value. **A buffer smaller than your pixel is not a
scale — it is a rounding error.** If you want a genuine multi-scale analysis,
your radii must be several times the cell size, or you need finer data.

**How to choose.** From biology, before you look at the results: how far can
this animal see, smell, or remember? For buffalo in savanna, a few hundred
metres to a couple of kilometres is defensible. What you must *not* do is fit
the model at ten radii and report the one with the smallest p-value — that is
a garden of forking paths, and the "optimal scale" it finds will not
replicate.

If scale genuinely *is* your question, there are principled multi-scale
approaches — but you have to say so in advance.
:::

## Task 5 — Time-matched annotation

Static covariates are easy. Now the one that actually matters.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
prec <- rast("data/kruger_prec_monthly.tif")
nlyr(prec)
#> [1] 12
names(prec)
#>  [1] "prec_01" "prec_02" "prec_03" "prec_04" "prec_05" "prec_06" "prec_07"
#>  [8] "prec_08" "prec_09" "prec_10" "prec_11" "prec_12"
```
:::


Twelve layers: the long-term average precipitation for each calendar month.
Kruger has a strong wet/dry seasonality, so this is a real seasonal signal.


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
plot(prec[[c(1, 4, 7, 10)]], col = hcl.colors(50, "Blues", rev = TRUE), nc = 2)
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![](exercise_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-16-1.png){fig-align='center' width=864}
:::
:::


The naive approach — one layer for everything:


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
static <- terra::extract(prec[[1]], pts)[, 2]   # January, for all fixes
summary(static)
#>    Min. 1st Qu.  Median    Mean 3rd Qu.    Max. 
#>    94.0    97.0   102.0   103.5   111.0   116.0
```
:::


The correct approach — **each fix gets the layer for its own month**:


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
month_idx <- as.integer(format(trk$t_, "%m"))

all_months <- terra::extract(prec, pts)[, -1]   # one column per month
matched <- all_months[cbind(seq_len(nrow(all_months)), month_idx)]

summary(matched)
#>    Min. 1st Qu.  Median    Mean 3rd Qu.    Max. 
#>    5.00   19.00   33.00   45.44   72.00  105.00
```
:::


::: {.callout-important}
## The indexing trick

`all_months[cbind(row, col)]` is matrix indexing: it picks element
`[row_i, col_i]` for each `i`. That single line is the whole of time-matched
annotation. For a real NDVI time series you would build `col` with
`findInterval()` against the layer dates instead of `format(t, "%m")`.
:::

### Your turn

**5a.** How different are the static and time-matched values?
**5b.** Do the buffalo experience more or less rain than the landscape average?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Solution


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
cmp <- data.frame(static = static, matched = matched)
round(cor(cmp, use = "complete.obs"), 3)
#>         static matched
#> static   1.000  -0.417
#> matched -0.417   1.000

cmp |>
  summarise(mean_static = round(mean(static, na.rm = TRUE), 1),
            mean_matched = round(mean(matched, na.rm = TRUE), 1),
            mean_abs_diff = round(mean(abs(static - matched), na.rm = TRUE), 1))
#>   mean_static mean_matched mean_abs_diff
#> 1       103.5         45.4            58
```
:::



::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
par(mfrow = c(1, 2))
plot(static, matched, pch = 16, cex = 0.2, col = adjustcolor("#1f6f78", 0.2),
     xlab = "January value (static)", ylab = "Value for the fix's own month",
     main = "Static vs time-matched")
abline(0, 1, col = "firebrick", lty = 2)

boxplot(matched ~ month_idx, col = "#1f6f78", border = "grey30",
        xlab = "Month", ylab = "Precipitation (mm)",
        main = "What the animals actually experienced")
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![](exercise_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-20-1.png){fig-align='center' width=816}
:::

```{.r .cell-code}
par(mfrow = c(1, 1))
```
:::


The two are barely related. The static version varies only in **space**; the
matched version varies in space *and* time, and the temporal swing here
dominates — Kruger's wet season delivers an order of magnitude more rain than
its dry season.

Any model using the static column would be answering "do buffalo prefer
places that are wet **in January**", not "do buffalo respond to rainfall".
Those are different questions, and they can easily give opposite answers.

::: {.callout-note}
These are long-term monthly *climatologies*, not the actual weather of
2005–2006. They carry the seasonal cycle but not the year-to-year anomaly. For
real work you would use a dated product — MODIS NDVI composites, ERA5
reanalysis, or Movebank's Env-DATA — and match on the actual date with
`findInterval()`. The mechanics are identical; only the layer dates change.
:::
:::

## Self-check

::: {.quiz}
You extract NDVI with `terra::extract()` and `summary()` reports a range of
−2000 to 9500. What is wrong?

- [ ] The raster is corrupt
- [x] You have raw stored integers — apply the scale factor, and handle the fill value
- [ ] NDVI can legitimately take these values
- [ ] The CRS is wrong

::: {.quiz-feedback}
NDVI is bounded by −1 and +1 **by definition** — it is a normalised
difference. Values in the thousands mean the product stores NDVI as scaled
integers to save space; MODIS uses a scale factor of 0.0001, so 9500 → 0.95.

The negative extreme is usually the **fill value** for missing data (MODIS
uses −3000), which must be set to `NA`, not multiplied. Leave it in and it
becomes a strongly negative NDVI at exactly the cloudy pixels where you had no
data.

Rule: after every extraction, `summary()` the new column and ask whether the
range is physically possible.
:::
:::

::: {.quiz}
Your study area straddles a national border and you stack a land-cover raster
from one country with a DEM from another. `c(dem, lc)` throws an error about
extents. What is the right fix?

- [ ] Crop both to their intersection and hope the grids align
- [x] `project()` to a common CRS if needed, then `resample()` one onto the other's grid
- [ ] Convert both to data frames and join by coordinates
- [ ] Use `extract()` separately on each and skip stacking

::: {.quiz-feedback}
Stacking requires identical CRS, extent **and** cell alignment. Cropping alone
fixes the extent but not the alignment — two 30 m grids offset by 7 m are
still incompatible.

`resample()` interpolates one raster onto the other's grid. Use
`method = "near"` for categorical data such as land-cover classes, or you will
invent classes that do not exist.

Extracting separately does work and avoids the problem, but only if you never
need the layers in a single object.
:::
:::
